spatial_claims.claim: A and B lie on both circumferences as distinct points of contact
O and Q are distinct centres of the two circles (by 3.6)
For internal contact, 3.11 places A on the produced line OQ
For internal contact, 3.11 places B on the produced line OQ
For external contact, 3.12 places A on segment OQ
For external contact, 3.12 places B on segment OQ
A, B, O, Q are all collinear
OA = OB (radii of circle centred at O)
QA = QB (radii of circle centred at Q)
O lies strictly between A and B (from OA = OB, collinearity, and O not on circumference)
Q lies strictly between A and B (from QA = QB, collinearity, and Q not on circumference)
Linear ordering A, O, Q, B along the line (after possible renaming)
AO is a proper part of AQ, so AO < AQ (CN5)
QB is a proper part of OB, so QB < OB (CN5)
AQ = QB (radii of Q) and OB = AO (radii of O), yielding AO < AO

configuration_map: All four points A, B, O, Q are collinear (Step 2). O is the centre of one circle with A, B on its circumference, so OA = OB and O is interior to its circle (not on circumference). Q is the centre of the other circle with A, B on its circumference, so QA = QB and Q is interior. From equal radii and collinearity, O must lie between A and B, and Q must lie between A and B (Step 3). With O and Q distinct and both between A and B, they can be ordered as A, O, Q, B (Step 4). This ordering produces the chain AO < AQ = QB < OB = AO, a contradiction.
pass_reason: The proof is a valid reductio ad absurdum. Each deduction step follows correctly: collinearity from 3.11/3.12, betweenness from equal radii on a line (via CN5), and the numerical contradiction from the linear ordering. The proof handles both internal and external tangency uniformly. No spatial configuration error exists; the contradiction is the intended conclusion of the proof by contradiction.
